pools.money_flow: Amazon pays about 3,000-4,400 small DSP businesses for last-mile delivery (DSPs employ the drivers), plus a smaller rural small-business delivery program, replacing volume that UPS is shedding.
pools.shock: UPS said on Jan 28, 2026 it is in the final six months of its Amazon glide-down, will remove another 1M pieces a day in 2026, cut up to 30,000 more jobs and close 24 more facilities after closing 93 in 2025. Amazon is spending about $4B to triple its rural delivery network by end of 2026 (200+ new delivery stations) and keeps expanding the DSP program.
pools.incumbents: Amazon Logistics (sole payer and rule-setter), UPS, FedEx, USPS. DSP owners earn per-route fees from Amazon.
pools.incumbent_fragility: The fragility sits with UPS (shrinking), not with a startup-addressable payer. DSP owners are price-takers; Amazon supplies vehicles, cameras, insurance and coaching, leaving little room for outside vendors.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: None found: searched 'startup serving Amazon DSP owners raises funding insurance payroll fleet software'. The absence likely reflects weak economics (single dominant payer, captive services) rather than opportunity.
pools.wedge_hints: Insurance, driver payroll/benefits and van financing sold to DSP owners; adjacent: small regional carriers absorbing volume UPS and FedEx prune. Honest limit: 4,000 DSPs times $25k a year of third-party spend is $100M at 100% share; only an insurance or financing product with $1M+ of premium or balances per DSP could work. Likely dead as a standalone (wrong-payer, lesson 3).
pools.insider_roles: DSP owners and station managers; Amazon last-mile program staff; UPS center managers; driver payroll providers; commercial auto brokers who write DSP fleets.

pools.name: US personal-auto physical-damage claims (collision + comprehensive): insurer payments for repair, parts, calibration and total-loss payouts
pools.size_basis: NAIC data via trade press: private-passenger physical-damage premiums about $154.3B in 2024 at a 59.9% loss ratio, so about $92B incurred losses (my arithmetic). Includes comprehensive, glass and theft, so the collision-shop revenue slice is smaller and not sized. NAIC report itself not opened.
pools.money_flow: Drivers pay premiums to insurers. Insurers pay repair shops (labor, paint, parts, ADAS calibrations), parts distributors and OEMs, and cash out total losses to owners. Estimating and valuation platforms (CCC, Mitchell/Enlyte, Solera) take per-claim fees.
pools.shock: 25% Section 232 tariff on non-USMCA auto parts effective May 3, 2025. CCC Crash Course 2026 (Mar 31, 2026, covering 2025): record 23.1% total-loss frequency, calibrations on 28.3% of repairable estimates (up from 21.8%), 72% of total-loss valuations on vehicles 7+ years old. Secondary: average repair cost $4,818, repairable claim volume -9.7%. Parts prices +3.8% and repair/maintenance +5% y/y in Apr 2026 (Scripps). NOTE: the widely repeated $3.4B / 2.7% tariff figure is a 2018 PCI projection, not current. An S&P headline claims a one-time $12B+ private-auto tariff hit (page not opened, unverified).
pools.incumbents: CCC Intelligent Solutions (public), Mitchell/Enlyte and Solera/Audatex own estimating, valuation and workflow. Insurers steer volume via direct-repair programs. Large MSOs (Crash Champions, Caliber, Gerber) are consolidating; Crash Champions renewed with CCC and expanded AI estimating in Aug 2026.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Insurer and shop are adversaries paying the same platform vendor, so neither can fix the other's incentives. Total-loss valuation (23.1% of claims) is the one step where the policyholder has no advocate. Each new calibration is a line item nobody in the chain owns. Tariff pass-through is slow and uneven across parts, and shops are squeezed between insurer-set labor rates and rising parts cost.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Revv ($20M Series A, about late 2024; AI inspections and supplier links for independent shops; lead investor conflicts between sources), ServiceUp ($55M Series B led by PeakSpan, Jul 2025; $70M total; fleet and insurance repair management), Tractable ($65M Series E, 2023; AI damage estimating), VaraFix (AI estimate review launched Aug 25, 2026; no funding disclosed), CrashBay ($1.25M, Apr 2024). Nothing funded found on ADAS-calibration networks or policyholder-side total-loss audit.
pools.wedge_hints: (1) ADAS calibration capacity and scheduling for shops. (2) Tariff-aware parts sourcing and price-lock for independent shops (PartsTrader is the incumbent to check). (3) Missed-operations and supplement audit for shops. (4) Policyholder-side total-loss valuation audit on contingency; check state total-loss rules and public-adjuster licensing. $100M revenue is about 0.11% of loss dollars, so a thin per-claim take works if one channel (large MSO or carrier program) is won.
pools.insider_roles: Collision shop estimators and owners, DRP managers at carriers, total-loss adjusters, ADAS calibration technicians, parts managers, public adjusters, auto-claims litigators.

pools.name: US consumer auto-loan interest and fees, with the subprime servicing, collections and repossession layer under stress
pools.size_basis: NY Fed Q2 2026 auto balances $1.713T times an assumed blended APR of roughly 7.5-8% (my assumption; Experian Q1 2026 originations average 6.39% new, 11.43% used, 21.77% deep-subprime used) gives about $130B interest a year. Subprime was 15.75% of Q1 2026 financing; subprime-only slice probably $40-55B (my estimate). Servicing/collections cost not sized from a source.
pools.money_flow: Borrowers pay interest and fees to banks, captives, credit unions, finance companies and buy-here-pay-here dealers. Lenders pay servicers, collection agencies, repo agents and auctions for servicing, recovery and remarketing.
pools.shock: Tricolor Holdings filed Chapter 7 on Sept 10, 2025 (alleged double-pledged collateral); Vervent took over servicing of about 100,000 loans within days. Fitch subprime 60+ day delinquency 6.9% in Jan 2026, reported as a record since the 1990s (vendor-cited; Philadelphia Fed argues it overstates new distress). NY Fed Q2 2026: 3.00% of balances flowed into 90+ day delinquency, most new serious auto delinquencies since 2010. Cox: about 1.73M repossessions in 2024, highest since 2009.
pools.incumbents: Captives and banks (Ally, Capital One, Santander Consumer, Credit Acceptance, Westlake; from memory), independent subprime lenders and BHPH dealers on legacy servicing systems (Megasys-type vendors), collection BPOs paid on recovery, successor servicers such as Vervent.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Independent subprime lenders have thin operations and fail abruptly (Tricolor), forcing emergency servicing transfers. Collection BPOs are paid on recovery, so they have no incentive to prevent default. Legacy servicing systems cannot do channel-level outreach or fast portfolio onboarding. Regulator enforcement pressure that used to fund compliance vendors has eased (my understanding, not sourced).
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Salient ($60M Series A, Jul 2025, loan-servicing AI; Axios Pro headline only, paywalled), Prodigal (AI collections for subprime auto; funding unverified), Vervent (successor servicer; ownership and funding unverified). No funded startup found focused on post-repo recovery, deficiency balances or a standing backup-servicing utility.
pools.wedge_hints: (1) Warm backup and successor servicing for small subprime lenders and ABS issuers (payers: warehouse lenders, ABS investors). (2) Early-intervention and extension programs priced per saved loan, below expected loss avoided (round 1 failed on this price/value test). (3) Post-repossession recovery and remarketing including deficiency balances. $100M revenue is about 0.08% of interest dollars.
pools.insider_roles: BHPH dealer principals, subprime collections managers, repossession agents and forwarders, auction remarketing managers, ABS investors and rating analysts (Fitch, KBRA), consumer-bankruptcy attorneys.

pools.name: US homeowners' residential HVAC replacement and installation (equipment plus labor)
pools.size_basis: AHRI 2025 shipments: 7.75M central AC and heat-pump units plus 3.25M gas furnaces (about 11.0M). Assuming 75-80% are replacements at about $6.5k average installed (both my assumptions) gives about $55B. Cross-check: Carrier CEO cited about 130M installed systems and about 6% replaced yearly, about 8M (secondary). Range $40-70B.
pools.money_flow: Homeowners pay local contractors (often under duress after a failure). Contractors buy from distributors, who buy from OEMs. Third-party lenders finance many jobs. Lead-gen platforms sit on the front end.
pools.shock: R-410A equipment manufacturing ended Jan 1, 2025 (A2L refrigerant transition; William Blair estimated 8-10% price increases). Section 232 tariffs on steel, aluminum and copper content. Federal 25C efficiency credit ended for installs after Dec 31, 2025 (contractor source; IRS page not opened). Result: 2025 central AC and heat-pump shipments -20.0%, with Oct and Nov 2025 down 49.4% and 46.4% y/y (partly pull-forward and a strong 2024 base).
pools.incumbents: OEMs (Carrier, Trane, Lennox, Daikin, Rheem and others), distributors, a very fragmented base of local contractors, some private-equity roll-ups (not sourced here), lead-gen platforms.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Homeowners buy with no price visibility and the comfort-advisor model depends on one-visit closes. OEMs cannot sell direct without breaking their dealer networks (channel conflict). Contractors face technician shortages and a post-credit, post-price-hike demand hole. Price opacity is the main thing a new entrant can attack.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Jetson ($50M Series A, Jan 2026, led by Eclipse; vertically integrated heat-pump installer, 1,000+ systems, CO/MA/NY and California from June 2026), Quilt ($20M Series B, date unconfirmed), Arch ($6.2M seed, date unconfirmed), Tetra ($10.5M seed, 2023), Aira (EU, EUR 150M). Field-service software incumbents such as ServiceTitan exist (not re-verified).
pools.wedge_hints: (1) Instant replace-on-failure quote, financing and install booking for conventional AC and furnace, sold on price transparency (the credit tailwind is gone and heat-pump startups are not focused here). (2) Contractor buy-side tools: price and availability across distributors, A2L compliance and refrigerant documentation. (3) Good-better-best quoting embedded at the distributor counter. $100M revenue is about 0.18% of the pool.
pools.insider_roles: HVAC contractor owners, comfort advisors and sales techs, distributor branch managers and counter staff, OEM territory reps, home inspectors, utility rebate program managers.

pools.name: US title insurance premiums (plus the attached settlement-fee stack)
pools.size_basis: ALTA 2025 market share analysis (published May 22, 2026): $18.5B premium, +13.8%. Claims paid just over $667M, about 3.6% of premium (my arithmetic). Top shares: First American 23.1%, Fidelity National 14.5%, Old Republic 14.0%, Chicago Title 13.1%, Stewart 10.9% (Fidelity and Chicago are both FNF brands, about 27.6% combined by my sum).
pools.money_flow: Buyers, sellers and refinancers pay premiums at closing to title agents and underwriters. The lender's policy is required; the owner's is optional. Agents keep most of the premium (typical split from memory, not verified).
pools.shock: Fannie Mae title-waiver pilot (started Nov 2024 with Doma, Westcor added Jul 2025; refinances under 80% LTV only; test ends Nov 30, 2027). FHFA Director Pulte said Fannie is working to expand it (reported Jun 26, 2026). KBW: pilot 'remains very small' and refinances are under 10% of title revenue. Fannie scrapped an earlier waiver pilot in Aug 2023 after industry pushback. The shock is real but modest so far; the pool matters because of the 3.6% payout ratio.
pools.incumbents: Five-brand underwriter oligopoly with thousands of independent agents; trade group ALTA, which has already defeated one waiver pilot. Rates are filed or, in some states, promulgated (Texas; from memory).
pools.incumbent_fragility: Any move toward pricing near expected loss would cut their premium base by an order of magnitude, and agents, who keep most of the premium, are their distribution. They cannot cut price or embrace waivers without destroying their own economics, so they respond with lobbying and risk arguments (First American study released alongside the expansion news).
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Titl (Miami, $2.5M seed, 2026), Qualia (closing software; Series D-II $40M Apr 2021), Endpoint ($150M corporate minority round, Oct 2021), Blueprint Title ($16M Series B, Sep 2021), Spruce (2018), Doma (pilot's first vendor; prior-wave underwriting-startup economics were poor, from memory). Very little funded in 2023-26.
pools.wedge_hints: (1) Automated title-risk scoring and attorney-opinion-letter workflow for low-LTV refinances, HELOCs and second liens, sold to lenders (budget line: closing-cost reduction and QC). (2) Consumer closing-cost transparency is a distribution wedge, not a revenue line. Check the legal premise first: state title-insurance statutes, rate filing and licensing, and whether the GSEs buy loans without a lender's policy beyond the pilot. $100M revenue is about 0.54% of premium.
pools.insider_roles: Title and escrow officers, underwriting counsel, agency owners, lender QC and closing managers, county recorders, real-estate attorneys in attorney-opinion states.

pools.name: US families' spend on paid child care (centers and family child care)
pools.size_basis: Committee for Economic Development / Conference Board: $68.5B industry revenue in 2022 (86% center-based, 624,300 businesses). Includes subsidy dollars. Child Care Aware 2025 national average price $13,184 per child (about 10% of median two-parent income, 33% for single parents). Parents' out-of-pocket share not found; EPI estimated $42B for under-5s in 2020. Probably higher now.
pools.money_flow: Parents pay (after-tax or pre-tax through dependent-care FSAs) or state subsidies (CCDF) pay about 624,300 providers, mostly small centers and home-based family child care.
pools.shock: Dependent-care FSA cap rises from $5,000 to $7,500 for tax years starting Jan 1, 2026 (law signed Jul 4, 2025). Section 45F employer child-care credit rises from 25% to 40% (50% small business) with cap $500k ($600k small), for 2026 expenses, and payments to intermediaries such as CCR&Rs now qualify. New Mexico began no-cost universal child care Nov 1, 2025, the first state. Supply is shrinking: home-based providers down 17,235 since 2019.
pools.incumbents: Tens of thousands of small providers, large chains (Bright Horizons, KinderCare; from memory), state CCDF subsidy administrators and CCR&Rs, DCFSA benefit administrators.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Razor-thin provider margins and low wages (center-worker average $28,185 in 2022) mean providers cannot raise price without losing families, and state subsidy rates lag cost. Subsidy payments are slow. Benefit administrators have no incentive to push employers toward the new 45F credit.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Brightwheel ($88.8M total; last round Series C, Feb 2021), Lillio/HiMama (Series B $55.6M, Nov 2021), Kinside ($12M, Jun 2022), Winnie ($9M, 2019), Upwards/WeeCare ($21M Series B, about Feb 2024), Bumo ($67M, Sep 2025; VCBacked only, unverified), Kidola ($2.5M, Jun 2025). Little aimed at employer-credit packaging or subsidy-payment speed.
pools.wedge_hints: (1) 45F intermediary product: an employer buys capacity or subsidies through a managed network and claims a 40-50% credit; payer is the employer's HR or finance head with the tax credit as the budget line (check how 45F treats for-profit intermediaries and whether employers will fund the cash outlay). (2) Fast subsidy reimbursement or payment advances for small providers. $100M revenue is about 0.15% of the pool.
pools.insider_roles: Center directors, family child-care owners, state CCDF administrators and CCR&R directors, employer benefits managers, child-care licensing inspectors.

pools.name: US private-pay in-home care for older adults (non-medical aides, companions, live-in)
pools.size_basis: LOW CONFIDENCE. IBISWorld puts 'elderly and disabled services' at $80.1B in 2025; Home Care Pulse reported agencies at 65% private-pay revenue in 2020 (down from 72% in 2018). 80.1 x 0.65 is about $52B (my derivation mixing scopes). NY DFS cites about $55B of total out-of-pocket long-term care in 2018, including nursing homes, so not like-for-like. Median aide pay $16.78/hour in 2024.
pools.money_flow: Older adults and families pay agencies (franchise and independent) or hire aides directly (household employment). Public payers (Medicaid, VA) draw on the same workforce.
pools.shock: OBBBA (Jul 4, 2025) cuts federal Medicaid by about $911B over 10 years (KFF); Medicaid pays about two-thirds of home- and community-based services; nearly one in three home care workers is an immigrant. DOL proposed (Jul 2, 2025) restoring the FLSA companionship/live-in exemptions for agencies and on Jul 25, 2025 halted enforcement of the 2013 rule (final status unconfirmed; many states require overtime anyway). TPS for Haitians ended after a Supreme Court ruling (reported Jul 2026), about 330,000 people, Haitians about 7% of the workforce per LeadingAge. CMS GUIDE dementia model: Papa joined Jun 2026.
pools.incumbents: Franchisors and independents (Home Instead, Right at Home, Visiting Angels and similar; from memory), thousands of local agencies, gray-market direct hires.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Labor supply is the binding constraint: immigration enforcement shrinks the pool as demand rises, and agencies cannot raise wages without pricing out families. Private-pay share is falling as public programs grow. Agencies run on referrals and local reputation with little tech.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Papa ($242M total; last big round Nov 2021; GUIDE partnership Jun 2026), Hera ($27M Series A, Jun 26, 2026, Bain Capital Ventures; coordination), Carallel (Series A-II about $2M, Jan 2025), Cariloop (Series C, Apr 2024), Wellthy ($25.5M Series C, May 2023), Hometeam and ConcertoCare (undated). Honor's $140M Series D appears to be 2021 (pre-window).
pools.wedge_hints: (1) Household-employer payroll and compliance for families that hire directly, cutting the agency markup (labor law varies by state). (2) Caregiver supply: training, credentialing, visa-eligible pipelines, backup-coverage pools. (3) VA Aid and Attendance and LTC-insurance claim filing for families. $100M revenue is about 0.20% of the pool, but unit economics depend on take rate against very tight labor supply.
pools.insider_roles: Agency owners and administrators, geriatric care managers, elder-law attorneys, hospital discharge planners and social workers, VA benefits advisors, state Medicaid HCBS program managers, immigration attorneys, aides themselves.

pools.name: US estate settlement (post-death administration) fees paid by estates and heirs
pools.size_basis: LOW CONFIDENCE; no authoritative national total exists. CDC provisional: 3,094,593 deaths in 2025. Assuming about half need formal administration (my assumption) at professional fees above $8,500 (WealthManagement) gives about $13B; the same article estimates North American hidden costs at $15-16B (author's estimate). Consumer guides cite 3-6% of estate value. Executor time is excluded: about 570 hours and 16 months average (EstateExec survey of about 1,200 adults); Alix cites 12-18 months and up to 900 hours. Realistic range $12-25B.
pools.money_flow: Estates and heirs pay probate and trust attorneys, CPAs (final 1040, 1041, 706), appraisers, real-estate agents, corporate trustees and courts. Funeral spend is a separate flow.
pools.shock: Cerulli projects $124T of wealth transfer through 2048 ($105T to heirs), with about $2.5T a year already inherited. The federal estate-tax exemption is $15M per person for 2026 deaths (OBBBA), indexed from 2027, so work shifts from tax planning to plain administration. Wealth managers are buying in to retain inherited assets: Alix's $20M Series A (Jul 2025, Acrew) included Charles Schwab and Edward Jones Ventures.
pools.incumbents: Fragmented small-firm probate bar billing hourly, bank trust departments, online will companies (LegalZoom, Trust and Will; from memory), state courts.
pools.incumbent_fragility: 50 state probate regimes and paper-based courts, and nobody owns the end-to-end job. Hourly billing rewards the 12-18 month timeline, so lawyers cannot easily productize. Banks, brokerages and insurers each handle thousands of death claims a year with no good intake process.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Alix ($20M Series A, Jul 2025; $30.65M total; Schwab and Edward Jones backing), EverSettled ($5M seed led by Emergence, reported Jul 17, 2026; CB Insights only, unverified), ClearEstate (Canada, CAD 16.8M Series A, 2021, pre-window). Empathy, Lantern and Cake not found in this search. Only Alix is well funded, and it owns the wealth-manager channel.
pools.wedge_hints: (1) Executor operating system with a flat-fee attorney network in high-volume states (CA, FL, TX, NY). (2) Deceased-account intake for banks, brokerages and insurers (payer is a servicing-cost budget line, not the grieving heir). (3) Real-estate disposition as the monetizing step. Legal premise to check: unauthorized-practice-of-law rules (Arizona ABS and Utah sandbox allow non-lawyer ownership). $100M revenue is about 0.67% of the pool and likely needs a channel partner rather than direct-to-heir marketing.
pools.insider_roles: Probate attorneys and paralegals, probate court clerks, bank trust officers and deceased-accounts ops staff, recent executors, funeral directors, estate-sale liquidators, fiduciary-return CPAs, life-insurance claims adjusters.

pools.name: US pet owners' spend on veterinary care
pools.size_basis: APPA 2026 State of the Industry: 'vet care and product sales' $41.0B in 2025 inside a $158B US pet industry (2026 projection $165B). Private equity spent $45B on vet deals 2017-2022 (PitchBook via Stateline); PBS reports vet costs up about 60% since 2014.
pools.money_flow: Owners pay mostly out of pocket (pet insurance is small) to clinics, increasingly corporate (Mars, NVA, Thrive; from memory and Stateline). Clinics buy drugs and diagnostics from Zoetis, IDEXX and distributors.
pools.shock: UK CMA final report (Mar 24, 2026): vet prices +63% over 2016-23 vs 31.3% inflation; remedies include price lists, prescription fee caps and a comparison site; online pharmacies 50-60% cheaper on common medicines (foreign precedent, not US law). In the US, Chewy closed its roughly $400M purchase of Modern Animal on May 21, 2026 (clinics 18 to 47), and telehealth VCPR laws are loosening (Rhode Island signed Jun 23, 2026; Arizona effective Sep 12, 2026; about 8 states). No US FTC action on vet consolidation found.
pools.incumbents: Mars Petcare (VCA, Banfield, BluePearl), NVA, Thrive and other PE-backed groups; Petco; Chewy Vet Care; Zoetis and IDEXX upstream.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Corporate groups earn margin on drugs, diagnostics and bundled pricing, which is exactly what price-transparency and prescription-portability rules attack (as the CMA is doing). Debt-funded roll-ups cannot cut price, and a vet shortage limits capacity.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Modern Animal ($46M, Sep 2025; then acquired by Chewy for about $400M), Supertails (India, $30M Series C, Feb 2026), Vetster ($30M Series B, 2022, pre-window), Invetx ($60.5M Series B, undated), PetPharm (Korea, Series B 2025), Chewy Vet Care (incumbent entrant).
pools.wedge_hints: (1) Buying group and services for independent clinic owners resisting or exiting a roll-up (valuations were 2-10x per Stateline). (2) Price-comparison and estimate-transparency layer on the model the CMA mandated. (3) Written-prescription portability to online pharmacies (check state law). $100M revenue is about 0.24% of the pool.
pools.insider_roles: Independent clinic owners, practice managers, vet techs, veterinary M&A brokers, compounding pharmacists, pet-insurance claims adjusters, emergency-hospital managers.

pools.name: US individuals' tax-preparation fees (paid preparers; DIY software not in the sourced figure)
pools.size_basis: IBISWorld: $15.0B for US tax preparation services in 2026. About 54% of individual returns for tax year 2021 were paid-prepared (GAO 2024, quoted secondhand). H&R Block FY2026 (June 30, 2026) revenue $3.95B, +4.9%; FY2027 guidance $4.11-4.16B. DIY software (Intuit and others) adds an unsourced amount; total probably $20B+ (my estimate).
pools.money_flow: Taxpayers pay paid preparers (H&R Block, Jackson Hewitt, CPAs, enrolled agents, independent shops) or DIY software (Intuit and others). Bank products (refund transfer fees) ride on top.
pools.shock: The IRS told the 25 participating states in Nov 2025 that Direct File will not run in the 2026 season, with no launch date set. It accepted 296,531 returns in 2025, more than twice 2024. Free File remains (AGI $89,000 or less). The 2025 budget law directed a task force on public-private partnerships to replace it. New 2025-law deductions (tips, overtime, seniors, car-loan interest) add complexity (not separately sourced). Honest read: the shock helped incumbents; H&R Block assisted revenue rose on higher net average charge and volume.
pools.incumbents: Intuit (TurboTax) and H&R Block hold the consumer layer along with the Free File partnership; Jackson Hewitt; CPAs and enrolled agents; thousands of independent shops.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Not fragile on price; the gaps are segments they under-serve (1099 and gig filers, multi-state filers, ITIN filers, simple filers who paid because the free option was hard to find). The IRS-built free option is gone, so a state-level or privately funded free/low-cost option is now an open lane.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Filed ($17.2M seed, May 2025; pro-facing), Fifteenth ($8.25M seed, Feb 2025; founders and tech employees), TaxGPT ($4.6M seed, Feb 2025), Taxwire ($25M seed or Series A, Jun 2026; single aggregator, unverified), TaxScouts (UK Series A). Column Tax: funding not confirmed. Funding clusters in pro-side AI tools, not consumer filing.
pools.wedge_hints: (1) White-label state free-filing (the Direct File architecture) sold to state revenue departments; budget line is the state DOR e-file program, and the federal task force may add demand. (2) Embedded filing inside payroll, gig-platform and banking apps for 1099 filers, sold per return. (3) Enrolled-agent network for simple-but-not-DIY returns. $100M revenue is about 0.67% of the sourced $15B pool.
pools.insider_roles: Enrolled agents, seasonal preparers and franchise owners, VITA coordinators, state DOR e-file managers, Free File Alliance participants, refund-transfer bank product managers.

pools.name: SNAP benefits redeemed at US grocers, plus state administration and retailer compliance spend
pools.size_basis: USAFacts: federal government spent $101.7B on SNAP in FY2025. Average benefit $188 per person per month. Participation about 39.5M in Dec 2025, down from about 43M a year earlier (unlabeled USDA table). The revenue pool for a vendor is administration plus retailer compliance, a small fraction of this figure.
pools.money_flow: Federal government funds EBT cards. Recipients spend at about 250,000 authorized retailers (count not verified). EBT processors (for example FIS in South Dakota) and POS vendors sit in the middle. States pay administration costs.
pools.shock: OBBBA (Jul 4, 2025) cuts SNAP by about $186B over 2025-2034 (CBO). States pay up to 15% of benefits from FY2028 scaled by payment-error rate, and their share of administration rises from 50% to 75%. Food-restriction waivers began Jan 1, 2026 in IN, IA, NE, UT and WV, about 18 states approved, and a National Grocers Association letter (Apr 2026) cites 22 state pilots with thousands of unresolved product-classification questions. Retail trade groups estimate $1.6B initial losses. In Jun 2026 a federal district court ruled USDA exceeded its authority approving waivers for five states (appeal status unknown).
pools.incumbents: EBT processors, POS vendors, grocers' IT teams, product-data firms.
pools.incumbent_fragility: There is no single national SKU-level eligibility dataset; each state defines categories differently and retailers update systems themselves. State agencies face a new hard cost line (75% admin share and error-rate-based benefit share) with no tooling budget. Federal court ruling adds legal uncertainty for restriction-based products.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Propel (Fresh EBT) raised a $4M seed in 2017 and $12.8M Series A in 2018; no 2023-26 rounds found. No funded startup found on SKU-level eligibility or state error-rate reduction.
pools.wedge_hints: (1) SKU-level SNAP eligibility data service (UPC denied-product lists by state) sold to retailers, POS vendors and EBT processors. (2) Payment-error-rate reduction tooling (income and asset verification, duplicate-participation checks) for states that now pay up to 15% of benefits. Caveat: retailer ARPU is small and the buyer is government with long procurement cycles, so $100M realistically needs the state-agency payer.
pools.insider_roles: Grocery front-end and IT managers, convenience-store compliance leads (NACS), POS and EBT-processor product managers, state SNAP quality-control directors, USDA FNS retailer-management staff, food-bank benefits navigators.

pools.name: Indonesia: free-meals programme (MBG) money flowing from BGN through ~27,000 community kitchens (SPPG) to ingredient suppliers
pools.size_basis: 2027 draft budget Rp240T = $15.09B for 60.6M beneficiaries (finance minister, 14 Aug 2026; fetched). 2026 allocation Rp335T (~$21B), Rp153.2T disbursed by end-Sept 2026 (search summary only). Derived: Rp240T / 27,000 kitchens = ~$560k per kitchen per year; ~70% on ingredients (BGN-cited, search summary) = ~$10B/yr of ingredient purchasing. Private capital already sunk in kitchen buildings ~Rp54T.
pools.money_flow: Treasury -> National Nutrition Agency (BGN) -> per-meal payments to ~27,000 privately financed kitchens run by partners (foundations, police-linked groups, businessmen, Kadin) -> ~70% of kitchen budget buys eggs, chicken, rice, vegetables, oil, milk from farmers, traders, cooperatives and village firms (BUMDes; BGN requires purchasing via cooperatives/BUMDes) -> meals to schoolchildren, pregnant women, toddlers.
pools.shock: Aug-Sept 2026 crackdown and re-plumbing: 13 Aug 2026 BGN directive after Berastagi school poisoning (rapid test kits for every kitchen, teachers must reject unfit meals, negligent kitchen heads face dismissal); 12 Sept 2026 BGN announced its own raw-materials marketplace (beef, chicken, eggs, rice, cooking oil, milk) launching late Sept/Oct 2026 with association-vetted sellers; July 2026 pause on new kitchens (partners say up to Rp8.7T investment at risk, ~13,000 kitchens could stall); 1,276 kitchens shut for lacking hygiene certificate (SLHS); a 2026 IPB study found only 44% of sampled kitchens had SLHS. Programme scaled from Jan 2025 to ~57M beneficiaries.
pools.incumbents: No incumbent buyer; the state is a new payer. Money is captured by kitchen partners (many politically or institutionally connected), local wet-market traders, cooperatives and BUMDes, and banks financing kitchens (e.g., BSI Rp181B for 127 kitchens). BGN itself is now building a government commodity marketplace.
pools.incumbent_fragility: BGN is a young agency inspecting 27,000 sites manually with paper reporting; disbursement runs behind budget (~46% spent by end-Sept 2026); policy swings (pauses, new certificates, mandated suppliers) strand kitchen owners who carry bank loans; supply-chain readiness and hygiene compliance are admitted gaps. Rules are being added faster than monitoring capacity exists. Risk to any entrant: the state marketplace and mandated cooperative layer can squeeze private intermediaries, and the programme itself could be cut (2027 draft below 2026 allocation).
pools.funded_startups_already_here: None found for MBG-specific kitchen operations, food safety or procurement (searched English and Indonesian; found no startup names or VC rounds). Government is building its own marketplace. Adjacent Indonesian food-supply-chain startups (Sayurbox, Eden Farm, Chickin) exist from background knowledge, not verified this run.
pools.wedge_hints: (1) Kitchen operating system: menu costing to BGN cost cap, inventory, daily reporting in BGN format, SLHS certificate tracking. (2) Food-safety testing/certification/audit service for kitchens. (3) Working-capital finance for kitchens waiting on BGN disbursements, underwritten on the BGN payment stream. (4) Cold-chain and last-mile ingredient logistics to rural kitchens. (5) Tooling for cooperatives/BUMDes that kitchens are now forced to buy from. Bottom-up: $10B ingredient flow x 1% = $100M but needs near-universal kitchen coverage; SaaS $150/month x 27,000 = $49M at 100% share; testing $1,500/kitchen-year = $40M at 100% share; a $100M path needs 2-3 stacked layers or a balance sheet.
pools.insider_roles: SPPG kitchen heads and nutritionists (ahli gizi), BGN regional coordinators, school principals/UKS officers, village cooperative and BUMDes managers, egg and chicken traders, Puskesmas sanitarians, BPOM/Dinkes inspectors, BSI/BRI kitchen-loan officers.

pools.name: India: interest and fees households and small businesses pay on gold-backed loans (banks, NBFCs, informal)
pools.size_basis: Outstanding gold loans ~INR18.6 lakh crore in Mar 2026 (Experian/CRIF bureau data, +50% y/y), ~INR20 lakh crore by Sept 2026 (RBI governor sees no overheating) = ~$200-215B; blended yield ~10% (conservative; NBFC rates far higher than bank rates, 13% blend gives ~$26B) = ~$20B/yr interest. Figures conflict by definition: RBI bank-only series was only ~INR4 trillion ($43B) in Jan 2026. Mostly search-summarized, not fetched.
pools.money_flow: Borrowers (farmers, shopkeepers, small traders, households pledging family jewellery) pay interest and fees to banks and NBFCs (Muthoot, Manappuram, IIFL, SBI, HDFC, ICICI, Federal, South Indian) and informal pawnbrokers/jewellers; lenders vault the gold, value it with in-house appraisers and auction on default.
pools.shock: RBI 'Lending against Gold and Silver Collateral Directions, 2025' (notified 6 Jun 2025) had to be adopted by 1 Apr 2026: LTV caps 85% (to INR2.5 lakh) / 80% (to INR5 lakh) / 75% above, LTV must hold through tenor; bullet consumption loans capped at 12 months; gold handled at lender's own branches by own employees with secure facility; assaying/purity standards; formal auction SOP with empanelled auctioneers; INR5,000/day compensation for late release. Plus a gold price run-up (one outlet: peak ~$5,595/oz on 29 Jan 2026, then ~27% fall; single commentator, unverified) and NBFC share of retail gold loans rising from 28% to 40% in a year.
pools.incumbents: Muthoot Finance (market cap crossed INR1 trillion in Jun 2025), Manappuram (Bain Capital approved to take up to ~41.7%), IIFL, plus banks (SBI, HDFC, ICICI, Federal, South Indian) and informal pawnbrokers. They earn on branch networks, local trust, vaults and high NBFC yields.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Incumbents are strong, not fragile. The fragility is in the manual process underneath: staff appraisal, physical vaults, paper auctions, fake/under-carat gold fraud, and a thin price buffer if gold falls (one commentator says 7-8%). The own-branch/own-employee rule blocks doorstep and outsourced sourcing models, so incumbents' physical networks become a moat and startups must serve lenders rather than compete with them.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Rupeek (Peak XV-backed, >$164M raised; 2024 down round at ~INR1,785 crore valuation; profit after tax INR15 crore in H1 of the current FY; reportedly seeking $50M in 2026; works with Federal Bank, South Indian Bank, Axis; co-lending with Indian Bank). IndiaGold could not be verified. No 2025-26 closed rounds confirmed. Search summaries only.
pools.wedge_hints: (1) NPA/auction disposal marketplace built to the new RBI auction SOP. (2) Purity/appraisal tech (handheld XRF assaying, appraiser certification, evidence capture) which the Directions make mandatory. (3) Compliance tooling for banks' rural branches adding gold lending (secure-facility certification, continuous LTV monitoring). (4) Loan-takeover/balance-transfer rails as borrowers move from NBFCs to banks. (5) Cross-lender fake-gold and fraud intelligence. Bottom-up is assumption-heavy: if annual disbursals are ~2x stock (~$430B), a 0.25% service take is ~$1B and a 10% share is ~$100M.
pools.insider_roles: Branch gold appraisers at Muthoot/Manappuram, NBFC auction and collections heads, rural bank branch managers, small-town jewellers and pawnbrokers, BIS hallmarking-centre operators, lender internal-audit and compliance heads, gold refiners.

pools.name: Brazil: annual tax-compliance spend of companies (accountants, ERP/fiscal software, consultants, in-house teams) during the rebuild around the dual VAT (CBS/IBS)
pools.size_basis: Soft. Estimates conflict: FEA-USP 'over R$30B/yr'; IPEA-hosted study 0.75% of GDP = 'about R$50B' (~$9B) on older GDP (at current GDP 0.75% would be higher, maybe $15B+); Deloitte R$181B outlier not verified; FIESP says industry spends 1.2% of revenue on tax computation and payment. I use ~$9B (R$50B) as a floor-ish figure. Needs a primary source before any pitch.
pools.money_flow: Millions of Brazilian firms pay accountants (contadores), ERP and fiscal-document vendors (TOTVS, SAP, Senior, Sankhya, Omie, Conta Azul), tax consultancies and in-house tax teams to compute, invoice and file taxes; from 2026 they must re-engineer systems for CBS (federal) and IBS (state/municipal) VAT replacing PIS, Cofins, IPI, ICMS, ISS by 2033.
pools.shock: LC 214/2025 set IBS/CBS rules; 2026 is a test year with symbolic rates (CBS 0.9%, IBS 0.1% shown on invoices and offset against PIS/Cofins) and NF-e/NFS-e must carry new fields; full CBS charging from 2027; old and new regimes run in parallel until 2033 so every ERP must support both. One ERP vendor claims invoices without the fields are rejected from 3 Aug 2026 (unverified). Sources are vendor and law-firm blogs with commercial bias.
pools.incumbents: ERP vendors (TOTVS, SAP, Oracle, Senior, Sankhya), SME software (Omie, Conta Azul), accounting offices (contabilidade), Thomson Reuters, Wolters Kluwer, Avalara, Sovos; big firms use in-house tax teams.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Not a 'cannot respond' pool; incumbents will ship updates. Openings come from parallel regimes to 2033, regulations still being written (Comitê Gestor, Receita), and credit-tracking under the new non-cumulative VAT (a buyer's credit depends on the supplier having paid), which legacy customised ERPs and per-hour accountants handle poorly. Mid-market firms with no in-house tax team are the underserved segment.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Spedy (e-invoicing; revenue +33% in Q1 2026 on reform demand), Omie, Conta Azul, Contabilizei, Arquivei, Dootax, Avalara, Sovos (several from background knowledge). Found no 2025-26 funding rounds for reform-specific tax tech; not verified on Crunchbase.
pools.wedge_hints: (1) Tax-rules engine as an API for mid-market ERPs lacking one. (2) IBS/CBS supplier-compliance and credit-tracking monitoring. (3) Transition audits and credit recovery on contingency fees. (4) Distributors/retailers with heavy ICMS-ST complexity. (5) Simples Nacional/hybrid-regime optimisation. Bottom-up: if ~1M mid-market firms paid $1,000-2,000/yr, pool is $1-2B and $100M needs 5-10% share; risk that ERP vendors bundle it free.
pools.insider_roles: Tax controllers at mid-market distributors, SME accountants (contadores), ERP implementation consultants (TOTVS/SAP partners), state tax auditors (auditores fiscais), tributarista lawyers, Comitê Gestor/Receita working-group members.

pools.name: Brazil: farmers' annual crop-input purchases (seeds, fertiliser, crop protection), 72% bought on credit from retailers, manufacturers and cooperatives
pools.size_basis: Input-industry revenue R$112.7B in 2024 (~$20B at ~R$5.5/$), of which R$80.8B (72%) involved credit; resale channel R$44.3B of credit, direct sales R$22.7B, cooperatives R$13.8B; barter R$13B (CropLife Brasil/Markestrat mapping, Jul 2025). Distributor view (Andav, 2025): R$171B total revenue, R$105B inputs, different scope. CPR stock R$565B (year uncertain). Search-summarized, not fetched.
pools.money_flow: Farmers buy inputs from retailers (revendas), directly from manufacturers (Syngenta, Bayer, BASF, Nutrien, Yara, Corteva) and from cooperatives; repay at harvest in cash or grain (barter/CPR). Retailers fund themselves from manufacturer terms, banks and capital markets (FIDCs, CRAs).
pools.shock: Record agribusiness judicial-recovery (bankruptcy-protection) filings: 1,990 in 2025 (+56.4%, Serasa Experian) and 474 in Q1 2026 (+21.9%); retailers' own filings up 32.4% in a year (RGF); Agrogalaxy, Lavoro and Belagricola restructuring with ~R$5B creditor losses; private Plano Safra resources ~20% below last year; drivers are high interest rates, dollar-linked input costs, weaker soy/corn prices. Physical CPRs are shielded from recovery proceedings (Law 14.112/2020); a 2026 CNJ provision reportedly reinforces this (commentary, unverified).
pools.incumbents: Input retail chains and cooperatives (the real decentralised lenders, R$44.3B of credit through resale), manufacturers' direct sales, banks (Banco do Brasil, Sicredi), traders (barter).
pools.incumbent_fragility: Retailers lend without bank-grade data on a farmer's total debt, collateral and planted area, and are now both victims and transmitters of farm stress; they cannot fund more risk, and banks are pulling back. Credit is the centre of the market, so any tool that improves loss rates is directly monetisable.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Traive (~$48M raised; $20M round with Banco do Brasil CVC and Astella; ~$84M post-money; credit analytics/registry sold to input supply chains), Agrolend ($21M; works via resellers; applied for central bank licence). Others not verified. Rounds found are 2023-24; no 2025-26 raise found. Search summaries only.
pools.wedge_hints: (1) Farm-level credit and collateral monitoring (satellite plus registry cross-checks) sold to retailers/distributors as a risk tool. (2) Physical-CPR/barter origination and registry compliance to move retailers to legally safer structures. (3) Workout/recovery services for defaulted farm debt. (4) Receivables-purchase/FIDC infrastructure for mid-size retailers shut out of bank credit. Bottom-up: 1% of R$80.8B credit sales is ~$150M, but $100M needs a risk-product or spread on roughly R$30-40B volume, a large share, and balance-sheet lending into a defaulting sector is dangerous.
pools.insider_roles: Input-retailer credit analysts, cooperative agronomists, agribusiness bankruptcy lawyers and judicial administrators, FIDC managers, rural-credit officers at Banco do Brasil/Sicredi, grain-trading originators.

pools.name: Mexico: freight, customs-brokerage and trade-compliance spend on US-Mexico truck trade
pools.size_basis: Derived, assumption-heavy. US-Mexico trade was $872.8B in 2025 (+3.9%, BTS annual via AJOT). BTS shows ~$46.1B of US-Mexico truck freight in Sept 2025 alone, ~$550B annualised. Door-to-door cross-border logistics plus brokerage at 3-5% of goods value (my assumption, not sourced) = $16-28B; I use $20B. Needs a real freight-revenue source.
pools.money_flow: Importers/exporters (autos, electronics, appliances, agriculture) pay truckers, drayage carriers, freight forwarders (C.H. Robinson, Kuehne+Nagel, DHL, Expeditors, Uber Freight/Transplace) and licensed customs brokers (agentes aduanales, patente holders) for line-haul, border crossing, clearance, bonds and insurance.
pools.shock: Mexico put tariffs of up to 50% on Chinese and other Asian imports from 1 Jan 2026; a 2026 customs-law overhaul adds duties and steep liabilities to licensed brokers; US 25% tariff on goods not qualifying under USMCA; USMCA joint review (July 2026; no outcome found). Rules-of-origin/substantial-transformation scrutiny rising; carriers reported near-zero freight growth in 2025 and flat rates early 2026.
pools.incumbents: Fragmented licensed customs brokers (patente guild, mostly paper/phone workflows), thousands of small carriers and owner-operators, large 3PLs and forwarders (C.H. Robinson, Kuehne+Nagel, DHL, Expeditors, Uber Freight/Transplace).
pools.incumbent_fragility: New broker liability and origin rules raise compliance load on exactly the segment least able to automate. But the broker patente is a legal moat: a startup must partner with or acquire a broker rather than replace one, and big 3PLs have the volume. Fragmentation of brokers and carriers is the opening.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Nuvocargo (digital forwarder + customs broker; $5.3M seed, $12M Series A, $20.5M Tiger-led Dec 2021, $36.5M Series B 2023 at >$250M valuation; unverified $10M convertible June 2025; acquired YC-backed Mentum Nov 2025; launched Nuvo AI Mar 2026). Flexport and big 3PLs sell cross-border services. Search summaries only.
pools.wedge_hints: (1) USMCA origin-qualification and certificate management for mid-sized exporters and IMMEX plants. (2) Broker-liability, classification and audit-record tooling for agencies post-reform. (3) Drayage and border-capacity marketplace for small Mexican carriers. (4) Duty/tariff-engineering analytics for importers. (5) Financing for duties, bonds and freight at the border. $100M is ~0.5% of the $20B pool if revenue is gross freight margin, more if software fees only; take rates not yet mapped.
pools.insider_roles: Agentes aduanales and their pedimento clerks, IMMEX trade-compliance managers at maquilas, Laredo/Nuevo Laredo freight forwarders, drayage dispatchers, customs attorneys, plant logistics managers, bonded-warehouse operators.

pools.name: Nigeria: household and business spend on petrol and diesel for self-generation (generators)
pools.size_basis: Most-cited: $14B/yr on generator fuel (attributed to AfDB's Adesina / IMF in Nigerian press); $10B/yr (SEforALL, possibly Lagos-only); ~N16 trillion in 2023 on self-generation fuel. Excludes generator purchases, maintenance, downtime. I use $12B mid-range. Press quoting older estimates; verify at source. Search-summarized.
pools.money_flow: Households, shops, hospitals, factories and bank branches buy petrol/diesel and gensets (Mikano, Sumec Firman, Perkins distributors, local dealers) because grid supply from DisCos is unreliable.
pools.shock: NERC Net Billing Regulations published 3 June 2026 let prosumers sell surplus solar to DisCos; Electricity Act 2023 lets states run own markets; Band A tariff ~N220-225/kWh for a promised 20 hours with a Feb-Mar 2026 shortfall compensation directive; $300M Distributed Renewable Energy Fund (NSIA/Africa50, $25M World Bank) launched 21 Sept 2026; a solar-panel import ban was proposed and remains unsettled; fuel dollar-linked and volatile.
pools.incumbents: Fuel retailers and depots, genset importers/dealers, DisCos.
pools.incumbent_fragility: DisCos are financially weak and cannot deliver reliability; genset economics only held while solar plus batteries were expensive. Fuel suppliers cannot respond to a customer who no longer buys fuel.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Arnergy ($18M Series B incl. $15M extension, 2025), Starsight ($15M BII mezzanine, Mar 2026; 500+ sites, 36MW), Daystar, Rensource, Westa Solar; Sun King and CrossBoundary not verified in this run. Nigeria installed ~803 MW solar in 2025, second in Africa.
pools.wedge_hints: (1) Small-business (10-50 kW) solar+battery lease for pharmacies, cold rooms, print shops, clinics, underwritten on prior diesel spend. (2) O&M and monitoring across heterogeneous installs. (3) Embedded financing via banks and genset dealers. (4) Net-billing metering/settlement software for DisCos and prosumers. 1% of $12B = $120M, so ceiling is high; the real constraint is naira-risk asset finance, not market size.
pools.insider_roles: Facility managers at banks and hospitals, genset technicians, solar EPC installers, DisCo metering engineers, NERC tariff analysts, estate managers in Lagos and Abuja.

pools.name: Emerging markets: fees and FX margin migrants pay to send money home (US to Mexico; Gulf to South Asia, Philippines, Egypt)
pools.geography: Global South corridors (US-Mexico, Gulf-South Asia, Philippines, Egypt)
pools.size_basis: Remittances to low- and middle-income countries ~$685B in 2024 (World Bank); average cost 6.49% (Q1 2025, probably $200 benchmark). 6.49% x $685B = ~$44B at face; large transfers and digital players are cheaper, so I use ~$30B for the fee-plus-FX pool. Mexico received $61.79B in 2025 vs $64.75B in 2024, the first annual fall since 2013. Search-summarized.
pools.money_flow: Migrant senders pay a fee plus FX spread to remitters (Western Union, MoneyGram, Ria, Remitly, Wise), Gulf exchange houses, banks and wallets; recipients get the net.
pools.shock: US 1% federal excise tax on remittances funded by cash, money order or cashier's cheque (IRC section 4475; bank-account and US-card funded transfers exempt) effective 1 Jan 2026; proposed regs April 2026, comments closed 12 June 2026, no final rule found. Direct effect looks small (98.6% of Mexican remittances were electronic in Jan 2026; only ~1.2% cash/in-kind); larger drivers are US immigration enforcement. Mexico inflows fell 3.6% in Aug 2026.
pools.incumbents: Western Union, MoneyGram, Ria/Euronet, Gulf exchange houses, banks, PayPal/Xoom. Earn on cash-in agent networks and FX spread.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Not fragile in aggregate; cash-agent incumbents are being undercut by app-based players, and the cash-funded excise tax adds a small cost to the most cash-heavy flows.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Remitly, Wise, LemFi, Felix Pago, Nala, Wave and many others (background knowledge; not re-verified in this run).
pools.wedge_hints: Weak. Possible: cash-to-digital conversion in stores serving cash-heavy corridors; payout rails and compliance for Gulf-to-South-Asia worker wage-to-wallet flows; B2B payouts for platforms paying migrant workers. Recommend deprioritising.
pools.insider_roles: Exchange-house branch managers (UAE, Saudi), MSB compliance officers, corner-store remittance agents in Mexico, correspondent-bank relationship managers, Gulf labour-recruitment agents.

pools.name: India: health-insurance claims that insurers pay to hospitals and patients
pools.size_basis: IRDAI annual report, FY2024-25: 32.6M claims settled, INR94,248 crore paid (~$10-11B at ~INR90-92/$), up from INR83,493 crore; 87% settled, 8% repudiated, 5% pending; average payout INR28,910; cashless ~66% of claim value; TPAs handled ~69% of claims by number (fetched, IndiaMedToday citing IRDAI). Govt said INR26,037 crore of claims rejected in FY2023-24 (search summary).
pools.money_flow: Policyholders pay premiums to general and standalone health insurers (Star Health, Niva Bupa, Care, HDFC Ergo, Bajaj Allianz, ICICI Lombard); insurers, often via third-party administrators, pay hospitals (cashless) or patients (reimbursement).
pools.shock: Aug-Sept 2025: AHPI told North India hospitals to suspend cashless treatment for Bajaj Allianz from 1 Sept over unrevised tariffs, unilateral deductions and delayed settlements; truce in September with cost dispute unresolved. IRDAI pushing to 100% cashless with pre-authorisation in one hour and discharge approval in three. Bima Bharosa complaints rose 47,658 (FY24) -> 64,365 (FY25) -> 73,729 (FY26 to Feb). GST removed on individual health premiums 22 Sept 2025 (background knowledge, not verified).
pools.incumbents: Insurers, TPAs (Medi Assist and others), hospital insurance desks.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Adjudication runs on PDFs, call centres and hospital-by-hospital rate cards; hospital-insurer relations are adversarial and disputes are public. Risk: the public National Health Claims Exchange (NHCX) could commoditise the plumbing; I did not find its current status.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Medi Assist (listed TPA), Plum, Loop, Onsurity, Even (background knowledge, not verified this run). Hospital-side claims/RCM automation startups exist but were not named or sized.
pools.wedge_hints: (1) Hospital-side claims desk for 10-100-bed hospitals with no revenue-cycle team: pre-auth packaging, discharge documentation, dispute appeals. (2) Contingency-fee recovery of disallowed/short-paid claims. (3) Rate-card and deduction analytics for hospital chains/associations negotiating with insurers. Bottom-up is thin: disallowed + repudiated claims ~INR26,000 crore (~$3B); 20% recovery at 15% fee = ~$90M at 100% penetration. Medium-quality pool.
pools.insider_roles: Hospital billing and insurance-desk managers, TPA claim adjudicators and medical officers, insurer claims heads, hospital CFOs, NHA/state PM-JAY agency officers, IRDAI grievance staff.

pools.name: Saudi Arabia: construction contracts issued by the state and PIF to contractors, now collapsing (distress and working-capital pool)
pools.size_basis: Saudi Contractors Authority: contracts issued under $30B in 2025, almost 60% below $71B in 2024 (and $113B in 2023); PIF share fell from ~38% (~$27B) to 14%. MEED Projects shows a different level ($164B in 2024 to $84.5B in 2025), so level depends on source, direction does not. Knight Frank: construction/transport/power/industrial output $148B in 2024. I use $30B (2025 awards ceiling) as the live flow. The pool is shrinking. Search-summarized.
pools.money_flow: Project owners (PIF and giga-projects such as NEOM, ministries, Aramco, private developers) pay main contractors (Webuild, Hyundai, Saudi Binladin, Nesma and others) who pay subcontractors and materials suppliers (steel, cement, MEP) and labour camps housing migrant workers.
pools.shock: PIF cut spending across its portfolio from early 2025 and giga-project schedules slipped; NEOM terminated large contracts (a ~$1B tunnel contract in March 2026; Hyundai and Webuild rail terminations); one report says NEOM's 2026-30 budget includes SAR60B ($16B) for contractor termination payouts vs SAR40B for new infrastructure (single source, unverified); Saudi bank lending growth reportedly slowed by more than half in Jan-May 2026; an Aug 2026 AGBI piece links Gulf contract disruption to an Iran war (details not verified).

Search summaries only.

(3) Receivables financing for tier-2/3 subcontractors on state obligors once SAMA rules settle. (4) Procurement for contractors trading down to cheaper materials. Money is mostly one-off settlements and working capital, not recurring spend; I found no path to $100M recurring revenue without balance-sheet risk on state counterparties. Know about, probably do not build.

pools.name: US farmers' annual purchases of fertilizer, lime and soil conditioners
pools.size_basis: USDA ERS farm income forecast (page updated Sept 3, 2026): fertilizer, lime and soil conditioners about $34.6B in 2025 and about $39.9B forecast for 2026 (both backed out from stated changes, so approximate); earlier ERS vintage put 2025 at $29.2B. Midpoint used.
pools.money_flow: Farmers pay ag retailers and co-ops (Nutrien Ag Solutions, CHS, independents), who buy from producers and importers (Nutrien, Mosaic, CF Industries, Koch, Yara, OCP).
pools.shock: Early-2026 Iran war pushed nitrogen sharply higher (one farmer's reported price went from $530 to $950 a ton within days). DOJ was reported investigating fertilizer price coordination in March 2026, the FTC confirmed a probe in May, and 17 farm groups asked the Senate Judiciary Committee to press DOJ in July.
