pools.size_basis: USDA ERS cash labor of $44.3B in the 2026 forecast; the broader labor line was $54.3B in the Sept 2025 forecast and farmdoc daily puts hired labor near $49B in 2023. The H-2A slice is about $12B (my arithmetic: about 391,600 positions requested in FY2024 x about $18.12 an hour x an assumed 1,200 hours, plus about $10,000 non-wage cost per worker).
pools.money_flow: Farm employers pay workers, plus recruiters, farm labor contractors, H-2A agents, housing and transport providers.
pools.shock: DOL interim final rule of Oct 2, 2025 changed how the H-2A Adverse Effect Wage Rate is set, using BLS OEWS data with two skill levels and a housing adjustment, because USDA discontinued the Farm Labor Survey on Aug 31, 2025 and the 2023 AEWR rule was vacated on Aug 25, 2025. UFW sued Nov 21, 2025. The notice cites a study of a possible loss of about 225,000 farm workers from enforcement.
pools.incumbents: Farm labor contractors, state grower H-2A associations, immigration attorneys and payroll providers capture the money through fees and markups on a paper-heavy process across about 2M fragmented farms.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Fragmentation and manual compliance: most employers run H-2A on paper and agents, and the wage-setting rules just changed under litigation, so incumbents' playbooks are unsettled. No single incumbent controls the channel.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Seso ($25M Series A from Index in 2022; $26M Series B led by BOND in April 2024), Croft ($2.67M seed, Feb 2024). No 2025-26 rounds found.
pools.wedge_hints: Employer-provided H-2A housing (the AEWR housing adjustment changes the economics); H-2A compliance and recruitment for mid-size growers; payroll, banking and remittances for farmworkers; ag workers' comp; harvest and packhouse automation sold as a service; wage benchmarking against the new OEWS-based rates.
pools.insider_roles: Farm labor contractor owners, H-2A agent-association staff, farm bureau labor directors, state workforce agency job-order staff, HR managers at growers with 1,000+ workers.

pools.name: US federal crop insurance premiums (farmer-paid plus taxpayer subsidy)
pools.size_basis: USDA RMA Summary of Business, 2025 crop year, interim snapshot as of Apr 21, 2025: total premium $18.04B, subsidy $11.26B (farmer-paid about $6.78B, my subtraction), liability $177.0B, indemnity $17.66B. The administrative and operating reimbursement to insurers is not sourced for 2025 (CRS: $1.6B in 2009, scales with premium); my estimate is about $2B or more.
pools.money_flow: Farmers pay about a third of premium; Treasury pays the premium subsidy and an administrative and operating reimbursement to Approved Insurance Providers, who sell through private agents. Treasury also reinsures losses and shares gains under the Standard Reinsurance Agreement; indemnities flow back to farmers.
pools.shock: One Big Beautiful Bill Act raised buy-up premium subsidies 3-5 points (38-64% to 41-69%), lifted the Supplemental Coverage Option subsidy from 65% to 80%, adds 90% coverage via the Enhanced Coverage Option in 2026, extra beginning-farmer support, and an extra 6% reimbursement in high-loss states (farmdoc daily, dollar value unverified). RMA implemented it by bulletin on Aug 20, 2025, effective for sales closing dates on or after July 1, 2025. CBO scores +$4.4B over 10 years; farmdoc argues earlier RMA actions on ECO added $13.2B.
pools.incumbents: About 16 Approved Insurance Providers (an older, roughly 2018-era count) sell identical federally priced policies through private agents; per a Watts analysis (2018) nearly all of the reimbursement goes to agent commissions.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Moderate. RMA sets rates and subsidies, so AIPs compete only on service and distribution; agent books, paper-heavy claims and a thin adjuster workforce are soft spots. Barriers to entry are real: AIP approval, capital and reinsurance.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: None found building a federally reinsured AIP or agency (searched Arbol, Descartes, Pula, Acre and general crop-insurance startups). Arbol (parametric, $60M Series B April 2024, about $250M gross written premium in 2023) is supplemental. Descartes, Pula and Acre returned nothing relevant for US farms.
pools.wedge_hints: Remote-sensing and drone claims adjusting sold to AIPs; digital agency or agent-book roll-up; SCO/ECO decision tools; supplemental private coverage layered on federal policies; specialty-crop MGA. A $100M path needs roughly 5% of a ~$2B reimbursement pool, so it is a roll-up or digital-AIP outcome, not a pure software one.
pools.insider_roles: Crop insurance agents with large books, AIP claims managers, loss adjusters, RMA compliance reviewers, farm lenders who require coverage.

pools.name: US feedlot and packer purchases of cattle and calves (cattle cash receipts)
pools.size_basis: USDA cattle and calves cash receipts of $134B in 2025, up 19% from $112B in 2024 (final figures, April 2026 summary, as relayed in search results; I did not open the document itself).
pools.money_flow: Packers pay feedlots for fed cattle; feedlots pay cow-calf ranchers and auction barns for feeder cattle; Mexican feeder cattle historically filled part of the gap.
pools.shock: Beef cow herd at 27.6M head in the Jan 2026 inventory, the lowest since 1951. New World screwworm closed the Mexican feeder-cattle trade (about $1.2B a year); 42 US cases as of about August 2026, nearly all in Texas; USDA announced a phased reopening on July 24, 2026 (Douglas, AZ from Aug 24 at 700 head a day, then 900, RFID required). Tyson announced closing its Lexington, NE plant in Nov 2025 (about 5,000 head a day, 7.5-9% of slaughter capacity) after a $1.135B FY2025 beef loss. USDA's Ranchers First Initiative (Aug 31, 2026) adds a heifer-retention insurance endorsement with no rollout date.
pools.incumbents: A few large packers (JBS, Tyson, Cargill, National Beef), large feedlots, and tens of thousands of cow-calf operations and auction barns.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Packers are losing money with excess capacity and a shrinking herd, and ranchers are undercapitalized to rebuild. The structural squeeze (cost of cattle versus slaughter capacity) is hard for incumbents to fix quickly.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: None found in the US for herd-rebuilding finance, EID/traceability or screwworm compliance (searched cattle fintech, marketplace and traceability startups). Nearest is France's EDS (Bovicash, EUR100M cattle-leasing platform, launching autumn 2026). Public money dominates: USDA's screwworm grand challenge had about $105M against about $664M requested.
pools.wedge_hints: Heifer leasing and herd-rebuild finance, possibly tied to the new heifer insurance endorsement; screwworm and EID compliance logistics at ranch and border scale; feeder-calf sourcing for feedlots; custom-grazing marketplace; brokerage of small regional packing capacity. Leasing carries mortality and regulatory risk.
pools.insider_roles: Auction market owners, order buyers, feedlot risk managers, ag bank and Farm Credit lenders, accredited large-animal vets.

pools.name: US electric utilities' spend on vegetation management (line clearance)
pools.size_basis: Harris Williams (2022) put it at about $8B and a 2026 Power Magazine piece at about $7B; no government total exists. Cross-check: Davey Tree 2025 revenue was $1.95B with Utility Services up 5.4% (about $54M); Asplundh is private with a secondhand $5.7B revenue estimate that includes non-vegetation work.
pools.money_flow: Utility operating budgets, recovered in rates, pay line-clearance contractors for trimming, tree removal, herbicide and work planning.
pools.shock: January 2025 Los Angeles fires: investigators pointed to Southern California Edison equipment for the Eaton Fire and LA County and DOJ sued SCE; California inverse condemnation imposes strict liability; property insurers are retreating; industry argues for a move from fixed trim cycles to risk-based work. NERC FAC-003-5 has applied since Apr 1, 2024. Davey reported a 37.9% ($10.2M) decline in its Utility Resource Group in 2025 tied to vegetation management market challenges, so demand is not uniformly strong.
pools.incumbents: Asplundh (private), Davey Tree (public), Wright Tree (employee-owned) and utility in-house crews, paid mostly by volume (miles cleared, trees removed) under unit-price contracts.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Business-model conflict: contractors are paid by volume, so risk-based programs that cut billable work run against their revenue. Labor shortages and rising contractor costs are cited, and utilities increasingly need regulator-grade evidence of work done.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Overstory (satellite/AI vegetation intelligence; sources conflict, with a reported EUR14M round in 2023 and a $5.2M round led by Convective Capital), Pano AI (wildfire detection, $44M Series B reported June 2025), Vibrant Planet (about $45M raised in total).
pools.wedge_hints: Independent post-trim LiDAR audit of contractor work for utilities and regulators; risk-based work planning sold with outcome data; hazard-tree prioritization; biomass disposal and wood utilization marketplace; contractor labor staffing.
pools.insider_roles: Utility vegetation program managers, utility arborists, contractor general foremen, work planners, wildfire-mitigation-plan regulators.

pools.name: US packaging extended producer responsibility (EPR) producer fees
pools.geography: United States (California, Oregon, Colorado, Maine, Minnesota, Maryland, Washington)
pools.size_basis: BORDERLINE against the $5B bar. California's first Circular Action Alliance program plan (filed June 15, 2026) projects a 5-year budget of $9.3-17.2B, about $1.9-3.4B a year (my division). Oregon is reported at about $100M a year (one weak guide). No sourced national total exists; my estimate at maturity across the seven states is $4-7B a year, dependent on plan approval and the federal challenge to SB 54.
pools.money_flow: Consumer packaged goods brands and retailers pay annual fees to a producer responsibility organization (Circular Action Alliance), which funds municipal collection, MRF upgrades and recycling targets.
pools.shock: California's first EPR program plan was filed June 15, 2026 under SB 54 (litigation pending in federal court); Oregon sent first invoices in Jan 2026 (another guide says the program went live July 1, 2025, so dates conflict); Colorado's program starts in 2026; the next fee cycle, based on detailed 2026 supply reports, begins in 2027.
pools.incumbents: Circular Action Alliance (the dominant producer responsibility organization), haulers and MRF operators, and the CPG brands that pay. Cities currently carry much of the cost.
pools.incumbent_fragility: CAA is new and building data and payment systems from scratch; CPG brands lack SKU-level packaging data; haulers have a conflict between collection and landfill revenue and recycling goals.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: ForSURE (Utrecht, EPR compliance software, $3.6M total, seed Sept 2024); on the sorting side AMP Robotics ($91M Series D, Dec 2024) and Sortera. No sizable US producer-side EPR compliance round found.
pools.wedge_hints: SKU-level packaging data and fee reporting for CPG companies; eco-modulation optimization (redesign to lower fees); audit and dispute of producer-organization invoices; reuse and refill systems paid with fee credits; financing for MRF upgrades; recycled-content resin sourcing.
pools.insider_roles: CPG packaging engineers and sustainability directors, MRF operators, Oregon DEQ and Colorado CDPHE program staff, municipal recycling coordinators.

pools.name: US farmers' spend on equipment repair, maintenance and parts
pools.size_basis: USDA NASS Farm Production Expenditures lists 'farm supplies and repairs' at $24.0B for 2024; repair and maintenance alone was $18B in 2023 (a Senate Agriculture deck citing ERS, not checked against the ERS table). Lower figure used. PIRG separately estimates repair restrictions cost farmers $4.2B a year (advocacy estimate).
pools.money_flow: Farmers and custom operators pay equipment dealers, and a minority independent shops, for parts, labor and diagnostics.
pools.shock: FTC and five states (IL, AZ, MI, MN, WI) settled with Deere on July 8, 2026: 10 years of dealer-equivalent repair tools and software for farmers and independents, including parts pairing, and no retaliation. Deere also agreed in April 2026 to a $99M class settlement for repair payers since Jan 2018. Iowa's House passed a farm right-to-repair bill 70-18 in April 2026.
pools.incumbents: Deere, CNH, AGCO and Kubota dealer networks. One dealer anecdote: parts about 20% of revenue at about 35% margin, service about 10% at about 70% margin.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Business-model conflict: dealer profit is concentrated in service and parts, and the settlement removes the diagnostic-software moat that protected it. Manufacturers earn thin margins on equipment and rely on the aftermarket.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: None found for independent farm repair or parts marketplaces in 2025-26 (searched marketplace, used-parts and right-to-repair startups); an established used-equipment and parts ecosystem exists.
pools.wedge_hints: Dealer-equivalent diagnostics and subscription tools for mixed fleets; mobile technician network; independent shop parts procurement; remanufacturing; technician training; downtime insurance. Actual tool access is unproven until the order is entered and tested.
pools.insider_roles: Independent ag repair shop owners, dealer service managers, custom harvesters, large-farm shop managers, former OEM service engineers.

pools.name: US community water systems' mandated lead service line replacement and PFAS treatment capex
pools.size_basis: DISPUTED. On the AWWA basis: PFAS compliance $3.8-5.5B a year (relayed by secondary coverage) plus lead line replacement of $46B to over $90B nationally over about 10 years (about $4.6-9B a year), giving about $8-15B a year. On EPA's own basis: PFAS about $1.5B a year plus the LCRI at $1.47-1.95B a year in total, about $3B, which is under the bar. Midpoint of the AWWA range used.
pools.money_flow: About 50,000 fragmented community water systems pay engineering firms, contractors, treatment media and equipment suppliers, funded by ratepayers, state revolving funds and federal infrastructure money.
pools.shock: EPA announced May 14, 2025 that it would keep the 4 ppt PFOA and PFOS limits, rescind four other PFAS limits and extend deadlines; the formal proposal of May 20, 2026 would move PFOA/PFOS compliance from April 26, 2029 to April 26, 2031 for systems that ask. The Lead and Copper Rule Improvements date stays Nov 1, 2027; oral argument in the AWWA v. EPA challenge was Sept 30, 2026, with a decision likely in 6-12 months.
pools.incumbents: Engineering and design firms, utility contractors, and treatment media and equipment makers; utilities themselves buy through slow municipal procurement.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Fragmented buyers and incomplete service line inventories. Deadlines and rules are moving under litigation, so incumbents face demand-timing risk, not a technology threat.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: BlueConduit (predictive lead-line identification; $2.25M across 5 rounds per an aggregator, last seed July 2023). No 2025-26 rounds for lead or PFAS water startups found in search.
pools.wedge_hints: Turnkey lead-line replacement programs for small and mid utilities that solve homeowner consent and access; inventory verification data; state revolving fund grant and loan navigation for small systems; PFAS treatment sold as a service (media change-out and regeneration). Timing risk from the PFAS delay and LCRI litigation.
pools.insider_roles: Utility water-quality managers, state SRF program managers, GAC and ion exchange media suppliers, public works directors.

pools.name: US biofuel producers' purchases of fats, oils and grease feedstock
pools.size_basis: EIA July 2026 monthly feedstock use (million lb): soybean oil 1,687, corn oil 453, canola 330, tallow 771, poultry fat 34, yellow grease/UCO 610, other 101, about 3,990 total, or about 48B lb a year at that run rate. At an assumed $0.50-0.60 a lb (my assumption; current prices not verified) that is about $24-29B.
pools.money_flow: Renewable diesel and biodiesel producers buy soybean oil, tallow, used cooking oil, corn oil and canola oil from crushers, renderers, collectors and importers.
pools.shock: EPA finalized 2026-27 Renewable Fuel Standard volumes in late March 2026 (published Apr 1): 9.07B gallons of biomass-based diesel for 2026, about 60% above 2025 (one source gives 8.95B for 2027, so figures conflict). From 2026 the 45Z credit applies only to North American feedstocks, and from 2028 imported feedstock and fuel get half the RFS value. UCO imports fell 38% year on year (China-origin down 67%), and biofuel's share of US soybean oil use is about 54%, up from 40% two years earlier.
pools.incumbents: Large renderers, crushers (ADM, Bunge, Cargill), thousands of fragmented UCO and grease collectors, and the refiners that buy.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Supply of domestic fats is inelastic in the short run and collection is fragmented, so scarcity rent goes to whoever controls domestic collection and origin documentation; imported-feedstock fraud and certification burdens favor traceable supply.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: None found in feedstock sourcing or traceability (searched renderer, UCO collection and feedstock traceability startups). Capital-heavy at scale, with strong incumbent renderers.
pools.wedge_hints: Grease route-density consolidation with software; origin and carbon-intensity documentation for 45Z and ISCC audits; waste-oil brokerage with North American origin certification; carbon-intensity measurement for soybean growers; offtake for new oilseeds (camelina, carinata, pennycress).
pools.insider_roles: Renderer procurement managers, UCO route collectors, refinery feedstock buyers, RIN traders, carbon-intensity auditors.

pools.name: US purchases of metal scrap by mills, smelters and foundries (ferrous and copper)
pools.size_basis: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026: domestic purchases of iron and steel scrap $19.7B in 2025 ($20.4B in 2024). Copper: 160kt from old scrap plus 760kt from new scrap, about 920kt contained copper at 490 cents a lb (about $10,800 a ton), about $9.9B (my arithmetic). Total at least $29B, before aluminum and other metals.
pools.money_flow: Generators (auto shredders, demolition, fabricators) sell to dealers and processors, who sell to mills, brass and rod mills, foundries and exporters.
pools.shock: Section 232 copper proclamation of July 30, 2025: 50% tariff on semi-finished and derivative copper from Aug 1, 2025 (scrap, cathode and concentrate exempt) and a direction to Commerce to pursue domestic sales requirements, including 25% for high-quality copper scrap (no implementing rule found; no scrap export controls imposed). A phased refined copper tariff (15% from Jan 1, 2027, 30% in 2028) was tied to a Commerce report due June 30, 2026. Refined copper imports jumped to about 1.7Mt in 2025 from 0.9Mt, with year-end stocks of 450kt and net import reliance of 57% (USGS).
pools.incumbents: A few large processors (USGS: five leading processors handled 26M tons through 354 facilities in 2023) plus a long tail of independent yards; exporters and domestic buyers have opposed interests in any sales mandate.
pools.incumbent_fragility: A possible domestic sales mandate and tariff-driven shifts in demand pit exporters against domestic mills; the long tail of independent yards runs thin, mostly manual operations with little software.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Sortera ($30.5M Series C, alloy sorting), AMP Robotics ($91M Series D, Dec 2024), Redwood Materials ($350M, Nov 2025, battery materials), Metaloop (EUR16M, 2023), ScrapAd (Spain, EUR6M Series A, Dec 2025, B2B scrap marketplace). No dominant US B2B scrap marketplace found.
pools.wedge_hints: B2B marketplace and price discovery for fabricators selling new scrap; chain-of-custody and grading certification if a domestic sales mandate is implemented; yard software (weighing, ID checks, payments); alloy-sorting as a service; fabricator scrap financing and hedging.
pools.insider_roles: Scrap yard general managers, mill scrap buyers, brass mill metal managers, metals brokers, shredder operators, customs brokers.

pools.name: NY CDPAP: New York Medicaid consumer-directed home care paid through a single fiscal intermediary
pools.size_basis: Reported program cost of about $9B a year with about 280,000 consumers (Spectrum News, Jan 2025, quoting the state). Advocates call the PPL contract $11B; that is a characterization, not used for sizing.
pools.money_flow: NY Medicaid (state + federal) pays a fiscal intermediary, which pays personal assistants (often family or friends) chosen by disabled and elderly consumers.
pools.shock: On 1 April 2025 Public Partnerships LLC (PPL) became the sole statewide fiscal intermediary, replacing roughly 600-700 FIs, after a federal TRO on 31 March forced continuity of pay. Hochul claims more than $1B saved by Jan 2026 (FPI says about $500M is clearly admin savings); advocates claim 150k workers and 90k consumers left (contested, unverified).
pools.incumbents: PPL, now the statutory single FI. Advocates allege private-equity control and service failures (unverified). About 700 displaced small FIs lost their model.
pools.incumbent_fragility: A single politically exposed state contract; the state wants savings and a working program at once and cannot quickly swap vendors, so friction builds at the edges. Displaced FIs hold caregiver relationships and data.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: None found at the FI layer, which is closed by statute (no dedicated startup search was run for this pool). Adjacent funded home-care platforms such as Papa and Honor exist, from memory and not verified this session.
pools.wedge_hints: (a) Displaced FIs converting to licensed home care agencies and needing back-office tooling; (b) enrollment, timesheet and benefits-navigation help for caregivers and consumers layered on PPL; (c) the same financial-management-services function in the other ~45 states with self-directed Medicaid programs, which is the only route to $100M.
pools.insider_roles: Former FI owners and compliance leads, independent-living-center staff, Medicaid managed long-term care plan care managers, home-care payroll specialists, elder-law attorneys.

pools.name: England adult social care: council purchases from independent home-care and care-home providers
pools.size_basis: GBP 29.4B gross current expenditure on adult social care in 2024-25 (GBP 23.6B long-term support), converted at 1.30 USD per GBP. Averages: GBP 23.56 an hour external home care; GBP 1,185.55 a week residential or nursing.
pools.money_flow: Councils (council tax, central grants, NHS transfers) pay independent providers at council-set rates; providers pay care workers.
pools.shock: The overseas Care Worker visa route closed to new applicants on 22 July 2025 (in-country switching allowed until 22 July 2028). Skills for Care 2025/26: international arrivals into direct care fell from 105,000 (2023/24) to 50,000 to 30,000; British-national posts fell 40,000 in a year; vacancy rate 6.2% (about 96,000), a decade low. Employer NIC rise in April 2025 added cost (from memory).
pools.incumbents: Thousands of small providers plus groups (HC-One, Bupa, Care UK, from memory); councils as monopsony buyer; staffing agencies.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Providers cannot raise prices (council-set), cannot recruit abroad, and domestic supply is shrinking; the 2028 transition cutoff sets a clock.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Cera (about $150M combined debt and equity, Jan 2025; reported valuation above $1B from one aggregator), Birdie (GBP 24.7M Series B, older), Florence (shift matching, GBP 28.5M Series B, older).
pools.wedge_hints: Domestic pipeline (UK-born recruits and returners), sponsorship-transfer matching for in-country switchers before July 2028, pay-on-demand and retention tooling, commissioning tools that let councils price the true cost of care.
pools.insider_roles: Registered managers, care-home recruitment leads, council commissioners, immigration solicitors, payroll bureau staff.

pools.name: England social landlords' repairs and maintenance spend (housing associations, Awaab's Law era)
pools.size_basis: GBP 10B repairs and maintenance in the year to 31 March 2025 for private registered providers (GBP 3.9B capitalised), up 13% from GBP 8.8B; forecast average GBP 10.9B a year over five years; at 1.30 USD per GBP. Excludes council housing repairs, so the true pool is larger.
pools.money_flow: Tenant rents, grants and borrowing pay landlords, who pay contractors (Mears, Wates, Kier and similar, from memory) and in-house repair teams, who pay trades.
pools.shock: Awaab's Law phase 1 took effect 27 October 2025: emergency hazards within 24 hours and short deadlines to investigate and make safe damp and mould; more hazards added in 2026 and 2027. The government impact assessment shows only GBP 10.8M a year net cost to business, which the sector and an acknowledging official say vastly understates cost.
pools.incumbents: Large repair contractors and housing-management software vendors (NEC, MRI, Civica, from memory). Nineteen providers with 40,000+ homes hold 42% of units and 47% of turnover.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Schedule-of-rates contracts pay per job rather than per outcome; legacy systems cannot track new legal clocks; landlord margins are already stretched by rent caps.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Switchee (Mould iQ launched May 2025 with three housing associations covering 92,000 homes), Mobysoft (RepairSense and a damp-and-mould module), Aico (HomeLINK sensors), Made Tech. Funding amounts not found.
pools.wedge_hints: Compliance clock and Ombudsman-ready evidence trail for Awaab's Law cases; dispatch of sub-GBP 500 hazard jobs across small subcontractors; ventilation and mould-remediation crews as a service; contractor performance audit for landlords.
pools.insider_roles: Repairs managers and damp-and-mould leads at housing associations, contractor operations directors, Housing Ombudsman case officers, surveyors.

pools.name: German Mittelstand ownership succession: purchase-price flow plus advisory and financing fees
pools.size_basis: Derived: KfW Nachfolge-Monitoring 2025 reports about 109,000 successions a year planned through 2029 at an average intended sale price of about EUR 499,000, giving about EUR 54B (about $62B at 1.15). This is an upper bound: not all are sales and the price is owners' hope. IfM Bonn expects about 37,200 actual handovers a year (reported, unverified), roughly EUR 18B. The capturable fee and financing layer is about 3-8%.
pools.money_flow: Successors pay retiring owners; Steuerberater, M&A boutiques, banks (Sparkassen) and KfW take fees and interest.
pools.shock: KfW Jan 2026: for the first time, planned closures without a successor (about 114,000 a year) exceed succession wishes (about 109,000). More than 2M owners are 55+; 42% of firms planning closure cite bureaucracy (+12 points); employee and management buy-outs are being considered by 28% and 24%.
pools.incumbents: Tax advisers (Steuerberater), Sparkassen and Volksbanken, IHK/HWK succession advisers, M&A boutiques, nexxt-change (free state-backed board), KfW loans.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Free public substitutes price matching at zero; advisers skip sub-EUR 1M deals; information is hidden and valuations are opaque; many firms are too low-earning to sell.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: None found with a 2023-2026 round in Germany. Historical: Carl Finance (EUR 3M, 2019), Valuedesk (EUR 5M, 2024, valuation SaaS), UnternehmerTUM ETA programme (Sept 2025). US analogs now funded: Baton, Rowan, Iconic.
pools.wedge_hints: EBO/MBO financing with KfW and Bürgschaftsbank guarantees; buy-and-hold vehicles for the roughly 114,000 planned closures; Handwerk trades (about 1M firms); valuation benchmarks. A $100M revenue path needs $1.5-3B of transacted value.
pools.insider_roles: Steuerberater, IHK and HWK succession moderators, Sparkasse corporate-client advisers, notaries, business brokers.

pools.name: German live-in elder care (24-Stunden-Betreuung): household spend on Eastern European live-in carers via agencies
pools.size_basis: Derived and borderline: Federal Health Ministry working group estimates 100,000-210,000 live-in carers on a given day (200,000-420,000 a year with rotation); price above EUR 2,000 a month plus board and agency fees. 100,000-210,000 x EUR 2,000-3,000 x 12 = EUR 2.4-7.6B; midpoint about EUR 5B (about $5.8B). Low confidence, wide range.
pools.money_flow: Households (topped up by Pflegegeld and the EUR 125 a month Entlastungsbetrag) pay a German placement agency plus an Eastern European posting company, which pay the live-in carer.
pools.shock: BMG working group report (Nov 2024) finds working-time, rest-time and minimum-wage rules often not met and false self-employment common, and that even agency placement is no guarantee of a legal model; the Federal Labour Court counts on-call time toward minimum wage with 3-year back-claims. A draft Pflegeneuordnungsgesetz was published 5 June 2026 and a Bundestag lobby-register entry (22 Sept 2026) ties live-in reform to it; what the draft actually requires is unverified.
pools.incumbents: Placement agencies (about 60 in 2009, 266 by 2017, no minimum standards) and posting companies mostly in Poland and Romania; legal models (Entsendung with A1, employer model, self-employed) all carry risk.
pools.incumbent_fragility: A compliant model forces employment, on-call pay and rest time, raising cost sharply; agencies cannot pass it on without subsidy, and the gray market has no registry.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: marta (Berlin, EUR 6.6M seed Aug 2022, over 13,000 families), Pflegehelden (sold to Rigeto 2021, over 3,000 customers), ennie 24h. No 2025 round found.
pools.wedge_hints: Compliant-employment infrastructure (A1 admin, time recording, cross-border payroll); family-side financing bridging Pflegekasse benefits; a certification standard (DIN SPEC exists but does not protect households).
pools.insider_roles: Agency founders and dispatchers, Polish posting-company owners, Pflegekasse caseworkers, care counselors (Pflegeberater), labour-law attorneys.

pools.name: Japan municipal water-supply pipe and facility renewal spend
pools.size_basis: Health Ministry forecast: replacing at the current rate needs an average of JPY 1.8T a year over FY2021-2050 (about $12B at 150 JPY per USD), about JPY 500B more than the prior decade; pipes alone JPY 33.5T over 30 years. Sewers are additional and not sized. Surfaced via search summaries; the decn.co.jp article returned 404 on direct fetch.
pools.money_flow: Water bills and general-account transfers fund municipal waterworks bureaus, which pay contractors, consulting engineers and pipe makers.
pools.shock: The Yashio sinkhole in Saitama (28 Jan 2025) triggered a national inspection of large sewers older than 30 years: 297 of 621 km inspected showed exposed rebar or cracks needing repair within five years, and 72 km needed work within one year.
pools.incumbents: Municipal waterworks bureaus, consulting engineers, pipe contractors, pipe makers (Kubota, Kurimoto, from memory); AI diagnostics from Fracta Japan (with NTT Business Solutions in Kakegawa, 1,062 km, Nov 2025), Hitachi Systems, Marubeni.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Shrinking customer bases and water volumes, aging engineer workforces, and a fixed 40-year legal-life rule that does not match real pipe condition; replacement rate about 0.64% a year implies a roughly 156-year cycle.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: No 2025 venture round found for a Japanese water-pipe AI company (funding amounts not found). Corporate and research players: Fracta Japan, Hitachi Systems, Marubeni, Maeda/Sumitomo Mitsui/University of Tokyo inspection robot; Bwell Technology (Shenzhen) filed for a Hong Kong listing.
pools.wedge_hints: Condition-based prioritization to stretch asset lives; void and cavity detection behind sewer pipes; wide-area utility consolidation back-office; PFI and operator bundles. The buyer is municipal procurement, so a local partner is needed.
pools.insider_roles: Municipal waterworks engineers, sewer inspection contractors, pipe manufacturers' sales engineers, MLIT officials, consulting engineers.

pools.name: Japan shippers' spend on contracted road freight (multi-tier trucking subcontract chain)
pools.size_basis: Derived: about 63,000 truck operators (MLIT, undated) x JPY 264M average 2023 revenue (All Japan Trucking Association management analysis) = about JPY 16.6T (about $110B at 150 JPY per USD). Whole logistics market about JPY 24.2T for FY2023 per a secondary summary of MLIT data. 99.5% of operators have capital of JPY 300M or less.
pools.money_flow: Shippers pay prime carriers and forwarders, who sub-contract down multi-tier chains of small carriers.
pools.shock: On 1 Jan 2026 the Subcontract Act became the Act on Proper Transactions for SME Entrusted Businesses, widening coverage to companies above 300 staff; Trucking Business Act amendments require written contracts itemizing charges (including fuel surcharges) and an actual-carrier register; designated shippers must appoint a Chief Logistics Officer and file a first medium- to long-term plan by end of October 2026.
pools.incumbents: Yamato, Sagawa, NX, Fukuyama (from memory), over 60,000 small carriers, and forwarders earning layered intermediary margins.
pools.incumbent_fragility: The new laws attack intermediary margin and unpaid waiting time; small carriers lack compliance capacity; the driver overtime cap (the 2024 problem) shrinks capacity.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Hacobu (MOVO; JPY 700M in May 2025, cumulative above JPY 5.6B), T2 (autonomous trucking; JPY 5B pre-Series B Aug 2025, JPY 16.5B-plus cumulative per one July 2026 report). CBcloud not verified.
pools.wedge_hints: Compliance back-office for about 60,000 small carriers (contracts, itemized charges, registers); waiting-time and berth data for shippers' CLO plans due October 2026; accessorial-charge billing and collection.
pools.insider_roles: Transport managers (unko kanrisha), dispatchers at mid-size carriers, forwarder pricing staff, warehouse berth managers, JFTC and MLIT enforcement officers.

pools.name: Japan home-visit long-term care insurance payments to home-help agencies
pools.size_basis: MHLW FY2024 care benefit statistics: home-visit care cost JPY 1,214,189M (JPY 1.21T), up 5.1% year on year, about $8.1B at 150 JPY per USD. All long-term care cost is JPY 11.94T.
pools.money_flow: Municipal long-term-care insurers (half tax, half premiums) plus 10-30% copays pay home-visit agencies, which pay helpers.
pools.shock: The April 2024 cut to home-visit base fees (about 2-3%) was followed by record bankruptcies: 176 care-provider bankruptcies in 2025 (second straight record), 91 of them home-visit (third straight), 87% with fewer than 10 staff (Tokyo Shoko Research, via secondary summary). Villages with zero home-visit offices: 107 at end-2024 (Kyodo), 116 at end-2025, with 285 municipalities down to one office by June 2026.
pools.incumbents: Large chains (Sompo Care, Nichii, from memory), municipal social-welfare councils, thousands of micro-agencies.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Per-visit reimbursement leaves rural travel time unpaid; helpers are aging; a fee cut landed when wages needed to rise.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: CareMaker (about JPY 100M, Feb 2025, visiting-nurse SaaS), CareFran (care-plan platform, Dec 2025), EMC Healthcare (Jan 2026). No large round found for home-visit billing or records.
pools.wedge_hints: Roll-up of distressed micro-agencies with a shared back office; municipality-level shared helper pools and route optimization; claim optimization for treatment-improvement add-ons; foreign specified-skilled-worker caregivers (home-visit allowed from April 2025, from memory). Needs Japanese operator talent.
pools.insider_roles: Care managers, agency service managers, municipal long-term-care section staff, Kokuho-ren billing clerks, social-insurance labour consultants (sharoushi).

pools.name: Northeast US home heating oil retail (fuel, service contracts and installs)
pools.size_basis: Derived: EIA (via Fuel Oil News, Nov 2025) has about 5.0M US households (4.1M in the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic) using oil as main heating fuel, spending about $1,390 each per winter at about $3.50 a gallon, about $6.9B; plus service and installs (19% of Star Group revenue) and commercial and multifamily oil, so an estimated $8-10B. Household counts date to EIA's 2020 survey.
pools.money_flow: Homeowners pay local oil dealers for delivery, service contracts and installs; dealers pay terminals and wholesalers.
pools.shock: Star Group FY2025 10-K: net account loss 4.7% (3.6% in FY2023), gross losses 13.5%, with conversions explaining only about 1.3% of lost accounts. NY and CT raised the bioheat minimum from 5% to 10% on 1 July 2025 (RI 10% to 20%). NY's all-electric new-building law start was delayed on 12 Nov 2025 pending appeal. A $450M New England Heat Pump Accelerator began Feb 2026.
pools.incumbents: Star Group (largest, 5.5%-plus share, 406,400 full-service and 63,200 delivery-only customers, bought one oil and three propane businesses for $80.5M in FY2025) and a long tail of family dealers (trade group NEFI represents about 1,100 oil and propane providers).
pools.incumbent_fragility: Fixed route and truck costs against 3.6-4.7% net annual attrition create a density death spiral; owners are aging; trade groups lobby against heat pumps rather than converting.
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Dandelion Energy (geothermal; $40M Series C reported around late 2024; targets NY, CT and MA oil and gas homes). No venture-funded dealer roll-up or dealer-software startup found.
pools.wedge_hints: Buy dealers' customer books and convert them to heat-pump, hybrid and service contracts using the $450M incentives; delivery route and degree-day SaaS; dealer succession brokerage; financing for oil-to-heat-pump swaps at burner failure. A $100M path is about 60,000-70,000 customers via 15-25 acquisitions, with thin margins on a shrinking base.
pools.insider_roles: Dealer owners and office managers, oilheat burner technicians, terminal operators, NEFI and NORA staff, state energy-office program managers.

pools.name: US Main Street business sales: SBA 7(a) change-of-ownership financing and brokerage
pools.size_basis: SBA FY2025 7(a) approvals were $37B across 77,600 loans; change-of-ownership loans were more than $9B (23.6%, Coleman Report) or $8.29B and about 7,003 deals (CT Acquisitions); BizBuySell Q3 2025 had 2,599 closed deals worth $2.13B, about $8.5B annualized on its marketplace. The fee layer (brokers and lenders) is under $1B, so this fails the $100M-revenue test unless a wide stack is captured.
pools.money_flow: Buyers, mostly using SBA-guaranteed bank loans, pay retiring owners; brokers, lenders and closing professionals take fees.
pools.shock: SOP 50 10 8 (1 June 2025): at least 10% equity injection and seller notes count only on full standby, up to 50% of the injection. A citizenship rule effective 1 March 2026 (100% US citizen or national owners; not confirmed against the SBA notice). SOP 50 10 8.1 issued 14 Aug 2026, effective 1 Oct 2026: debt-service coverage on historical earnings only, quality-of-earnings report for deals of $3M or more, and 7(a) Small barred from ownership changes.
pools.incumbents: Live Oak Bank (top acquisition lender), Huntington, First Internet Bank; business brokers and the BizBuySell marketplace.
pools.incumbent_fragility: Lender-side rules now force re-underwriting and add cost and time on larger deals; brokers' listings priced around old financing assumptions may need repricing (my inference).
pools.funded_startups_already_here: Baton ($10M Series A, Jan 2025), Iconic ($6M seed, May 2026), Rowan ($3.3M seed, Mar 2026), DealFlowAgent (about $646K-750K, 2026), Boom ($3.3M seed), Acquire.com (older rounds).
pools.wedge_hints: Lightweight earnings normalization for sub-$3M deals (below the QoE threshold); seller-note standby servicing; non-citizen buyer alternatives. Honest verdict: real shock but small, crowded fee pool.
pools.insider_roles: SBA lender underwriters, business brokers, CPAs who do quality-of-earnings work, SBA closing attorneys.
